5.63.m: Śeṣa said: / Seeing Lava fainted, he who tears apart mighty foes, / Śatrughna of great strength attained victory at the forefront of the battle.
Placing the boy Lava, adorned with a helmet and other armour, upon his chariot, / he, who in form resembled Rāma, then desired to depart.
"Our friend has been captured by the enemy!"—thus, filled with sorrow, / the boys quickly reported to Sītā, his mother.
The boys said: / "Mother Jānakī, your son took by force the steed / of some foremost king who is proud and endowed with an army.
Then a terrible battle took place with his army, O Jānakī; / and then your heroic son struck down all of them.
After that, your charming son gained victory; / having caused that king to faint, he won victory on the field of battle.
Then, recovering from his faint, this extremely fierce king / became enraged and struck down your son on the field of battle.
He had previously been forbidden by us: 'Do not seize the excellent horse,' / but he held in contempt all of us, Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas."
Hearing these dreadful words of the children, / she fell to the lap of the earth and wept in her grief.
Sītā said: / "How is it that a king, devoid of compassion, fights with a child? / An evil-minded wrongdoer is he who struck down my child!
O heroic Lava, endowed with great strength, where are you? / Alas, why did you carry off the excellent horse of a merciless king?
You are a child, and they are overwhelming, skilled in all weapons. / They are mounted on chariots, and you are on foot; how could there be an equal battle?
My dear child, with you alone I had forsaken the grief of being abandoned by Rāma. / Now, deprived of you, long-lived one, how shall I live in the forest?
Come, release the sacrificial horse; let this lord of the earth go! / You, the wiper of my grief, do you not know my sorrow?
If Kuśa, that crest-jewel of heroes, had been in the battle, / he would now have rescued you from the side of the king.
Even he, due to my fate, is not near; what shall I do now? / Fate alone is indeed the cause of the arising of my sorrow."
Lamenting thus and in many other ways, the glorious woman / scratched the earth with her big toe, [weeping] with tears from both eyes.
She said to the boys: "Where is that child, and where will that king go / after striking down my son in battle?"
While this Jānakī, devoted to her husband as to a deity, was speaking these words, / Kuśa arrived from Ujjayinī accompanied by great sages.
Having worshipped Mahākāla on the fourteenth day of the dark half of Māgha, / and having obtained abundant boons from him, they arrived before the mother.
Seeing Jānakī agitated, overcome with tears springing from her eyes, / her voice faltering and piteous with grief, just as he was eager to speak,
at that moment his arm throbbed, foretelling battle, / and in the heart of that great car-warrior arose an eagerness to fight.
He replied to his mother, who was speaking piteously and with faltering speech: / "Mother, with me, your son, present, your grief is gone.
While I live, tears must not fall from your eyes to the ground." / Kuśa spoke to his mother, who was distressed by tears and speaking piteously with a faltering voice,
he, of steadfast mind, instantly feeling grief for her who was grieving: / "Where is my brother Lava, the crusher of enemies?
Always, knowing that I had arrived, he would come to my side rejoicing. / Why is the hero not seen? Where has the mighty one gone to play?
Or with whom has he gone, out of childishness, or to look for me? / Why are you weeping, mother? Where is Lava?
Tell me all that which is the cause of your grief." / Hearing those words of her son, the grieving woman said to Kuśa:
"Lava has been captured here by a certain king guarding the horse; / my boy bound the horse that was suitable for the sacrificial rite.
The mighty one, alone, conquered many enemies, its guardians; / then the king rendered him unconscious and bound him at the head of the battle.
The boys, his companions, have told me so; / therefore I became sorrowful upon hearing that Lava had been captured.
Deliver him by force from that foremost of kings, having arrived in time!" / Hearing his mother's words, Kuśa, filled with wrath, / spoke to her, biting his lip and grinding tooth against tooth.
Kuśa said: / "Mother, consider Lava freed from the bond of the noose! / Now I shall slay him together with his entire army and mounts with my arrows.
Even if a god or an immortal, or even if Śarva has arrived, / still I will release him from him with my sharp-jointed arrows.
Do not weep, mother; here, for heroes, fainting in battle / is indeed for glory; it is fleeing that brings dishonour.
Give me a divine coat of mail, a bow fitted with a bowstring, / a helmet, O mother, and a sharp sword.
I go now into battle; I shall strike down the great army; / I shall rescue my brother who has fainted in the midst of battle.
If I do not rescue your son from the great battle today, O mother, / then may both your feet be angry with me on this earth!"
Śeṣa said: / Pleased by these words, Jānakī of auspicious marks / gave him a host of weapons, endowing him with blessings of victory:
"Go, my son, to the battle; rescue the unconscious Lava!" / Thus commanded, the mighty Kuśa, clad in armour, wearing earrings,
wearing a diadem, holding a sword, carrying a shield and bearing a bow, / placed two inexhaustible quivers upon his shoulders that possessed the strength of a lion.
Having bowed to his mother's feet, the foremost car-warrior set out with speed, / as he went swiftly with great speed to the combat for the fight.
Just then he saw his own Lava striking down the enemy hosts. / The heroes, the mighty warriors, saw Kuśa approaching,
like Death arrived to destroy the entire universe. / Lava, seeing that his mighty brother Kuśa had arrived,
blazed exceedingly in battle like fire combined with wind. / And leaping down from his chariot, he went forth to battle.
Kuśa hurled in the eastern direction all the heroes stationed on the battlefield; / Lava in anger drove them all into the western direction.
Overwhelmed by the pain of Kuśa's arrows, afflicted by Lava's shafts, / all the men in the army, O sage, were tossed about like a surging ocean.
Tormented then by Kuśa and by Lava with volleys of arrows, / the entire army, filled with heroes, found no peace.
Broken in every direction, terrified again and again, / not a single warrior, though possessed of strength, wished to stand anywhere on the battlefield to fight.
At that moment, King Śatrughna, scorcher of foes, / marched to fight against the heroic Kuśa, who was just like Lava.
Seeing Kuśa endowed with might, equal in splendor to Rāma's form, / standing in his golden chariot, the slayer of enemy heroes spoke.
Śatrughna said: / Who are you, resembling your brother Lava, endowed with immense strength? / What is your name, great hero? Who is your father? Where is your mother?
Why do you dwell in the forest frequented by twice-born sages, O bull among men? / Tell me everything so that I may fight with you, O mighty one.
Hearing these words, Kuśa spoke to the king / with a voice deep as thunder, making the battlefield resound:
“Sītā, devoted to her husband, brought us forth alone. / We dwell in the forest, dedicated to worshipping the feet of Vālmīki.
Zealous in serving our mother, skilled in all sciences, / we have become renowned as Kuśa and Lava, O sinless king.
Who are you, a hero praised in battle? For what purpose was the excellent horse released, / and today you are in battle, eager to conquer, accompanied by your army?
Fight with me if you are a hero, O king! / Now I shall fell you at the head of the battle.”
Śatrughna, knowing him to be the son of Sītā, born of Rāma, / marveled in his heart, yet in anger took up his bow.
Seeing him having taken up the bow, Kuśa, filled with rage, / strung his own very firm and excellent bow.
Śatrughna, knower of all weapons, released sharp arrows; / Kuśa cut them all down with ease, laughing aloud in the battle.
Hundreds of thousands of arrows of Kuśa and of the king / covered the entire world; that, O sage, was wondrous.
With the fire weapon, the mighty Kuśa swiftly burned them all; / the valiant king extinguished it with the rain weapon.

The king of great prowess extinguished it with the wind weapon; / then a fierce wind arose all around the circle of battle. / With the mountain weapon he checked that wind which was causing agitation.
With the thunderbolt weapon the king cut down those rocks in the battle. / Then the powerful Kuśa released the Nārāyaṇa weapon; / but it could not harm King [Śatrughna], the devotee of Nārāyaṇa.
Then, exceedingly enraged and overcome with fury, / Kuśa spoke to King Śatrughna of mighty strength and prowess:
“I know you to be a great hero who achieves victory in battle, / since my terrible Nārāyaṇa weapon did not harm you.
Now I shall fell you to the earth today, O king, with three arrows; / if I do not do this, then hear my vow:
He who, having attained a human body difficult to obtain even through ten million merits, / disregards it out of delusion—may his sin be mine in this matter!
Be vigilant here upon the field of battle; / I fell you instantly to the earth!” Having spoken thus, onto his bow
he fitted a terrible arrow shining like the fire of destruction, / aiming at the enemy's broad, hard, and mighty chest.
Seeing that arrow aimed, Śatrughna, frantic with rage, / released sharp arrows capable of piercing Kuśa's skin.
That arrow indeed flew forth to pierce his heart, / terrible in form, equal to fire, hissing like a venomous serpent.
Remembering Rāma, the excellent king quickly aimed at that arrow / and severed the sharp-jointed shaft released by Kuśa.
Then Kuśa, exceedingly enraged by the severing of his arrow, / placed another sharp-jointed shaft upon his bow.
As he, mighty and exuberant, prepared to pierce his chest, / he severed before that his arrow shining like the fire of destruction.
Then Kuśa, remembering his mother's feet, filled with rage, / placed a third, wondrous arrow upon his bow.
Śatrughna too swiftly took up an arrow to cut it down, / but before he could, pierced by that arrow, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
A great cry of lamentation arose when Śatrughna was struck down. / Kuśa, proud of the strength of his own arms, gained victory there.

5.64.m: Śeṣa said: / Seeing Śatrughna fallen, the excellent king Suratha / advanced, standing in a very wondrous chariot crafted of jewels.
Reflecting that Puṣkala had already been struck down in the battle, / he then advanced to fight Lava, who was lofty in the strength of a great hero.
Approaching Kuśa and releasing arrows in many ways, / Suratha, the crest-jewel of great heroes, caused affliction in the battle.
Kuśa deprived Suratha of his chariot with ten flaming arrows, / and swiftly cut down his very firm bow, fully strung.
With the hurling and counter-hurling, the discharges and counter-discharges of weapons, / there was a tumultuous battle that made the hair of the heroes stand on end.
While King Suratha, difficult to conquer, was intensely engaged in battle, / Kuśa pondered: “What must I do in this battle?”
Having reflected, endowed with immense strength, he took up a sharp, terrible arrow / to slay the king.
Seeing that incoming arrow shining like the fire of destruction, / he immediately resolved to cut it down, but the great arrow struck him beforehand.
Then the hero of great valor and strength swooned in the battle; / he fell upon the floor of the chariot, and the charioteer carried him away.
Seeing Suratha fallen and Kuśa victorious, / striking terror into the hosts of heroes, the son of the wind advanced.
Seeing the powerful monkey, the son of the wind, approaching, / Kuśa laughed, baring his teeth, as if angering him in fury.
And he said to Hanumān: “Come before me! / I shall pierce you with a thousand arrows; dead, you shall go to the night [of death].”
Thus addressed, Hanumān, knowing him to be the mighty son of Rāma, / ran forward, thinking: 'The master's work must be accomplished.'
Uprooting with force a huge śāla tree with a hundred branches, / the mighty one advanced to fight, aiming at Kuśa's chest.
As the mighty Hanumān approached with the śāla tree in hand, / the powerful Kuśa pierced him in the heart with three crescent-shaped arrows shining like the moon.
Swiftly struck by the arrow of the mighty Kuśa, / Māruti, grinding his teeth, struck him in the chest with the śāla tree.
Struck by the śāla tree, the boy did not tremble even slightly out of wonder; / then the heroes praised him for his youthfulness.
Struck by the śāla tree, that hero took up the Saṃhāra weapon; / out of anger Kuśa, the knower of supreme weapons, [took it up] to slay the enemy.
Seeing the invincible Saṃhāra weapon released by Kuśa, / [Hanūmān] meditated in his mind upon Rāma, the destroyer of obstacles for his devotees.
Then that weapon, swiftly discharged by Kuśa, / struck the heart of the son of Marut, causing great agony; thereby he fell once more into a swoon.
Seeing that monkey fallen into a swoon, the powerful [Kuśa] / pierced that entire vast army with sharp arrows.
Broken by his ten thousand arrows on the battlefield, / the entire army, complete with its four divisions, took to flight.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys and great protector, in wrath / uprooted many trees and rushed against the prominent Kuśa.
Laughing, Kuśa effortlessly cut down all the trees; / and again, the powerful one swiftly severed the oncoming trees.
Pained by numerous arrows on the battlefield, / Sugrīva seized a terrible mountain [aiming] at Kuśa's head.
Seeing that mountain approaching, Kuśa crushed it manifold / with arrows, swiftly making it fit to be an ornament on the body of Mahārudra.
Seeing that great deed accomplished by the boy, / Sugrīva's hope of victory vanished on the battlefield.
Overpowered in the midst of battle, beating with his tail, / Sugrīva, extremely impatient and overcome with rage, seized a tree to slay Kuśa.
Seeing Sugrīva intent on killing him, [Kuśa] vigorously / struck him with many sharp-jointed shafts.
Struck by various kinds of arrows and filled with pain, / he set out to slay Kuśa, went, and took up a śāla tree.
Even then, the heroic Kuśa, the elder brother of Lava, / took up the Vāruṇa weapon and bound him with a tight noose.
Bound with smooth cords by the mighty Kuśa, / he fell right in the midst of the battle adorned with great heroes.
Seeing Sugrīva fallen, the warriors fled in all directions; / Lava's brother, the crest-jewel of great heroes, attained victory.
Meanwhile, Lava, having conquered the warriors, Puṣkala and Aṅgada, / the foremost in valor, Vīramaṇi, and other kings as well,
having attained victory in battle, the heroic Lava went to his brother, / the author of victory in the fight, who had felled millions of foes.
Both rejoiced and embraced each other; / having attained victory, O sage, intoxicated [with joy], they conversed.
Lava said: / 'Brother, by your grace the ocean of battle has been crossed; / now let us inspect the splendid battlefield of heroes.'
Having spoken thus, the two heroes, Kuśa and Lava, went swiftly / and seized the king's wonderful diadem-jewel inlaid with gold.
The heroic Lava took Puṣkala's auspicious crown, / and the priceless [ornaments] of Aṅgada, and another of Śatrughna.
Gathering the collection of weapons, both approached / Hanūmān, the monkey lord, and Sugrīva, and bound them both.
Grasping the tail of the son of Vāyu, Kuśa's younger brother / said this to his brother: 'I will take him to my own dwelling.
Holding him by his tail, [I will take him] for our mother's delight, / for the play of the sons of sages, and for my own amusement.'
Having heard those words, Kuśa then said to Lava: / 'I shall take this strong, sturdy monkey.'
Speaking thus, those two bound those two foremost of the strong, / and holding the two powerful ones by their tails, they went toward their hermitage.
Seeing themselves going toward the hermitage, those two best of monkeys, / trembling, spoke to each other in fearful voices.
With a mind distressed by fear, Hanūmān said to the monkey king: / 'These two sons of Rāma are carrying us to their own hermitage.
Formerly, a deed was done by me when I went to Jānakī; / there the charming goddess Jānakī stood before me.
She, Vaidehī, will see me bound by an enemy with a noose; / then she will laugh, and great shame will be mine on this occasion.
What is to be done by me here? Giving up of life will occur. / And a great misfortune has befallen; what will that Rāma do?
Sugrīva, hearing his words, [said:] "So it is for me too, O great monkey; / if he takes me thus, death indeed will occur."
Even as the two were speaking thus to one another, terrified with fear, / Kuśa and Lava reached their mother's abode with vigor.
Seeing the two arrived, their mother rejoiced; / with supreme affection, she embraced her two sons mutually.
Seeing those two monkeys seized by their tails by the two [boys]— / Hanūmān and Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, heroic over all—
The excellent woman laughed, beholding the two bound with a noose, / and spoke, uttering an excellent word for the sake of [their] release:
"Sons, release the two monkeys, mighty heroes of great strength! / Seeing me, if they are distressed, they will abandon their lives.
This one is indeed the hero Hanumān, who burnt Danu's city; / this one is also the king of bears, indeed the earthly ruler of all monkeys.
Why were they seized? Where? Or what was done out of disrespect? / They were held by the tail by you two; great is my astonishment!"
Hearing their mother's gentle words and looking at her, her two sons, / possessed of great strength and supreme in humility, said:
"Mother, there is a certain king, the mighty Rāma, son of Daśaratha. / By him was released a horse adorned with a golden plaque on its forehead.
There was written thus: 'O mother, a mother of sole heroes is mine; / let those who are kṣatriyas seize [it], otherwise they are worshipers of the soles of my feet.'
Then indeed a thought was made by me in my heart, O devoted wife: / 'Is not the lady a kṣatriya woman, or would she not be a mother of heroes?'
Seeing that insolence of the king, the horse was seized by me by force; / it was conquered by the heroic Kuśa, and that army was struck down in battle.
Know this crown to be the king's, O lady to whom her husband is a deity; / this one also belongs to another hero, the high-souled Puṣkala.
Know yet another crown adorned with jewels and pearls; / this charming horse of the king is my desired steed.
Know it, O excellent lady, to be for my mighty brother to ride; / these two monkeys, best of the mighty, were brought by me to play with.
These two fighters in combat were [brought] just for your amusement!" / Hearing this speech, Jānakī, to whom her husband is a deity,
spoke to her two heroic sons: "Release them again and again!" / Sītā said: / "An injustice was committed by you two: the great horse of Rāma was taken;
many heroes were struck down, and these two monkey lords were bound. / The heroic horse belongs to your father; it was released by him for the sake of sacrifice.
Did you two take the horse even of him in the best of sacrifices? / Release these two monkeys! Release the best of horses!
Let the brother of the king, Śatrughna, who angers enemies, be forgiven!" / Hearing that word of their mother, the two strong ones said to her:
"By the law of the warrior caste we conquered that mighty king; / no injustice will be ours who fight according to the law of the warrior caste.
Formerly it was said by Vālmīki before us as we studied:
'Holding the horse suitable for sacrificial rites at Kaṇva's hermitage, / for that reason a son may fight even with his own father, and a younger brother with an elder brother,
or even a disciple with his teacher; therefore, no sin arises.' / And now, by your command, we two shall give the excellent horse;
we shall indeed release these two monkeys, and we will carry out your word." / Having spoken thus to their mother, the two heroes went to the battlefield [and] the two lords of monkeys
they released, and also the horse suitable for the horse sacrifice rite. / Goddess Sītā, hearing from her two sons that the army had been struck down,
meditating on Śrī Rāma in her mind, looked upon the sun as witness: / "If in mind, speech, and action I attend to the leader of the Raghu race
and in my mind to none other, then may this king live! / And may all this great army, which was forcibly destroyed
by my two sons, live by my truth, O Lord of the worlds!" / While Jānakī, to whom her husband is a deity, was speaking this word,
so long did all that force come to life at the head of the battle.

5.65.m: Śeṣa said: / In a moment the heroic Śatrughna recovered from his swoon on the field of battle; / the other mighty heroes also who had fallen into a swoon fully revived.
Śatrughna saw the best of horses standing before him, / and himself devoid of helmet, and the army revived.
Seeing this wonder, he reflected in his mind and spoke indeed / to Sumati, foremost of ministers, then freed from swoon:
"Having shown compassion, the boy gave back the horse for the completion of the sacrifice. / Let us quickly go to Rāma, who is eager for the horse's return."
Having said this, standing on his chariot and swiftly taking the horse, / he went far away from that hermitage, without kettle-drums or conchs.
Behind him the great fourfold army / marched, making the lord of serpents bruised by its weight.
Having swiftly crossed the Jāhnavī, billowy with waters, / he went into his own country, adorned with his own people.
Accompanied by Puṣkala, united with Suratha, / the king, standing in a gem-studded chariot, held a mighty bow.
Placing that horse before him, adorned with a garland of gems, / and a white parasol over its head, adorned with chowries,
surrounded by many thousands of chariots, by mighty kings / charming with raised bows, adorned with the battle-cries of heroes,
in due course he reached the city adorned by the solar dynasty, / decorated with many excellent banners and resplendent with fortresses.
Rāma, hearing that the horse had arrived together with that Śatrughna / and with the heroic Puṣkala, experienced manifold joy.
He ordered the camp and the mighty fourfold army; / he sent his brother Lakṣmaṇa, foremost of the mighty.
Lakṣmaṇa, having gone with the army, / overcome with joy embraced his arrived brother, whose limbs were adorned with wounds.
Having inquired about welfare everywhere, he made conversation here; / having attained supreme joy, Śatrughna met him with gladness.
Standing in his chariot together with his brother, the high-minded heroic son of Sumitrā / went toward his own city with the great army.
The Sarayū, having holy waters, purifies the three worlds; / purified by the dust of Rāma's feet, it has the luster of the autumn moon.
It is crowded with swans and ducks, adorned with ruddy geese, / and loudly made resonant by birds of various diverse colors.
Pavilions in great numbers were made there by Rāmabhadra, / resounding with the individual chanting of Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
Many kṣatriyas were there, well adorned with bows in their hands, / resounding the surface of the earth with the loud twanging of bowstrings.
Where Brahmins eat with various enchanting foods, / looking at one another, they held charming conversation.
Bright milk-rice preparations, equal to the splendor of the moon, / filled with much milk and ghee, and mixed with sugar;
many cakes were there, resembling the disk of the moon in beauty, / scented with the fragrance of camphor and other [spices], exceedingly charming;
crisp phenikā cakes, oily pots of delicacies, sweets with hundreds of holes and without pores, / śaṣkuli pastries, soft maṇḍaka breads, accompanied by sweet foods;
boiled rice white as a night-lotus, mixed with mung bean dāl, / accompanied by fragrance, giving extreme delight;
cooked rice mixed with curds, accompanied by Bhīmasena [seasonings], / prepared by skilful cooks and served in dishes by attendants.
Seeing the milk-rice placed in their dishes, certain twice-born men there / said to one another: "What is this wondrous thing that is seen?
Has the disk of the moon fallen from the sky out of fear of darkness? / For here is ambrosia, wondrous and destroying death."
Hearing that, another excellent twice-born, with eyes red with indignation, said: / "Indeed, this cannot be the disk of the moon overflowing with ambrosia.
The body of the moon is one; how could it be seen identically / in the dish of each of a thousand brāhmaṇas separately?
Therefore know that this must be a night-lotus or camphor; / do not consider it the disk of the deer-marked [moon] endowed with white splendor."
Meanwhile another, seized with anger, shaking his head, [said]: / "These foolish twice-born, unskilled in the knowledge of flavors, do not know!
This has been thoroughly cooked with the syrup of honey-bulbs; / know them to be the sweet petals of the lotus."
In this way, O sage, the brāhmaṇas who ate only roots and fruits / debated among themselves with delight, very greedy for the knowledge of flavors.
Then another twice-born said: "The birth of kṣatriyas is superior; / such food, prepared through great merits, is enjoyed by them."
Then a brāhmaṇa said to him: "Such is the fruit of giving; / those who give to the first-born attain their desired goal.
By those by whom Hari has never been worshipped again and again with varied offerings of food, / such an edible object can never come into the range of their eyes.
Those men by whom the first-born have been fed with diverse flavors / enjoy this delicious taste, which is hidden from the eyes of sinners."
Fed with sweet dishes possessing such flavors, / those best of the twice-born, experts in the Word-Brahman, recited in the pavilion.
Some danced, some laughed, some roared in great exhilaration; / a grand festival shone forth, and then Śatrughna arrived there.
Seeing Śatrughna approaching accompanied by Puṣkala, / Rāma was unable to contain the joy that arose then.
As soon as Rāma stood up [to welcome] his brother, the guardian of the horse, / Śatrughna, devoted to his brother, embraced Rāma's feet.
Seeing his brother, endowed with humility and his limbs adorned with wounds, / fallen at his feet, [Rāma], deeply pleased, embraced him tightly.
Shedding many tears of joy upon his head, Rāghava / attained an utmost, supreme joy that was beyond words.
Brought to tears of tenderness, he drew Puṣkala, who was bowing at his feet, / firmly between his arms and pressed him closely.
As well as the heroic Hanūmat, Sugrīva, and likewise Aṅgada, / Lakṣmīnidhi, the son of Janaka, preeminent in majesty, Ripuṃjaya,
Subāhu, the heroic Sumada, Vimala, Nīlaratnaka, / Satyavat, Vīramaṇi, and Suratha, the servant of Rāma,
And other exalted kings, who were affectionate and bowed at his feet, / Raghunātha himself then embraced firmly.
Having firmly embraced Śrī Raghupati, who shows grace to his devotees, / the pleased Sumati stood before [him] upright.
Then Rāma, the best of speakers, seeing his own minister / arrived in his presence, spoke to the counselor with supreme affection:
"O Sumati, best of ministers, best of eloquent men, tell me: / Who are all these kings, and how have they come here?
Where and where did the horse go? By whom and by whom was it restrained? / Or how was it freed by my brother, who is endowed with great strength?"
Śeṣa said: / Thus addressed, Sumati, the best of counselors, very wise, / smiling and with a voice deep as a thundercloud, spoke to Rāghava.
Sumati said: / "How can I speak today before you, who are all-knowing? / You ask according to the custom of the world, [yet] you, all-seeing, know everything.
Even so, placing your command always upon my head, / I speak; hear that today, O crest-jewel of all kings!
By your grace, O Lord, all over the surface of the earth / your steed wandered, beautifully adorned with the inscribed plate upon its forehead.
No one seized it, arrogant with pride in the strength of their own name; / having surrendered their respective realms, they bowed to your lotus-like feet.
Who indeed, desiring victory, free from old age and death, / would seize the excellent horse of the slayer of Rāvaṇa, king of the Daityas?
First your charming steed went to Ahicchatrā. / King Sumada of that [city], having heard that your horse had arrived, O Lord,
Together with his son, being powerful and surrounded by his entire strong army, / surrendered his whole kingdom, having removed all thorns.
Which king, having propitiated the Mother of the Universe, the ruler of the worlds, / obtained long life and a kingdom free of thorns—
that very Sumada bows to you, who are served by lords. / Receive him with a glance of mercy, he who has long desired your sight.
Then, in the city of King Subāhu, which was filled with strength, / his son Damana seized the excellent horse.
A great battle took place with him, with Damana; / and Puṣkala attained victory, having caused the son of Subāhu to faint.
Then Subāhu, enraged in battle, fought by force / with the son of the Wind, the servant of your lotus-like feet, best among the strong.
Struck by his foot, having gained knowledge and casting off his curse, / surrendering everything to you, he became a protector of the horse.
This King Subāhu of tall stature bows to you; / do you sprinkle Subāhu, who is skilled in policy, with your glance of mercy.
Then released, the horse plunged into a pool of the Revā; / there the Deluding weapon was obtained by the exceedingly strong Śatrughna.
Then it went to Devapura, which is adorned as the dwelling of Śiva. / But you know what happened there, since you yourself came there.
The Daitya Vidyunmālin was slain; then Satyavat joined [us]. / You know of the battle with Suratha, O great-minded one.
Then released from Kuṇḍalaka, the horse wandered everywhere; / no one seized it, arrogant with pride in the power of their own prowess.
The delightful horse arrived at the charming hermitage of Vālmīki. / What wondrous event happened there, hear that, O best of men!
There a sixteen-year-old youth, bearing your likeness, / seeing the horse marked with the inscribed plate, seized it, being exceptionally strong.
There a great battle occurred with Kālajit, O best of men; / he was slain by that hero with a sharp-edged weapon.
Many of great strength, Puṣkala and others, were slain in the battle; / and that crest-jewel of heroes also rendered Śatrughna unconscious.
Then the king, considering great sorrow in his heart in the battle, / in anger, that hero, the best of the strong, made [him] faint.
As soon as he was made to faint by the king, another [boy] arrived. / By that one and this one, reviving, your army was destroyed.
Having taken the weapons and ornaments of all who had fainted, / and having bound the two monkeys, they went to their hermitage.
Showing compassion, he gave back the great sacrificial horse; / and the entire army whose life was lost was brought back to life.
Taking that steed, we have arrived in your presence. / This is what was known by me; that has been spoken before you."

5.66.m: Śeṣa said: / When the two children in Vālmīki's hermitage had indeed been spoken of by Sumati, / realizing, "They are my sons," he addressed Vālmīki:
Śrī Rāma said: / "Who are those two children who bear my likeness, best among the strong? / For what purpose do they dwell there, skilled in the science of archery?
Hearing of the two mentioned by the minister, amazement arises in me: / they who playfully bound Śatrughna and Hanūmat!
Therefore, O sage, tell me the entire deed of the two boys, / so that my highest, wished-for delight may indeed come about."
Having heard that speech of the wise king of kings, / he spoke an excellent word composed of clear syllables:
Vālmīki said: / "For you, the Inner Ruler of men, how could there not be knowledge? / Even so, I speak here for the sake of your satisfaction.
O King, the two boys in my hermitage are the best among the strong, / bearing your likeness, having bodies that are charming in their limbs.
When Jānakī, truly innocent, was abandoned by you in the forest, / pregnant, lamenting again and again in the dreadful forest,
seeing your beloved, the virtuous daughter of Janaka, / stricken with grief like an osprey, I then brought her to the hermitage.
A charming leaf-hut was built for her by the sons of the sages; / in it she gave birth to two sons who illumined the ten directions.
I gave the names to the two clearly: Kuśa and Lava. / They grew there continuously like the moon in the bright fortnight.
In time, I performed all [the rites] such as the sacred thread ceremony; / I caused them to learn all the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, O King.
Hear all [their accomplishments] with their secrets from my mouth: / medicine, the science of archery, and likewise the science of weapons,
and then the Jālandharī lore; and they were made skilled in music. / Singing on the banks of the Gaṅgā and in the vine-bowers and forests,
the two were lively, active in mind, skilled in all sciences. / Then I attained immense satisfaction, O best of the Raghus!

Having given them all missiles, my hand was placed upon their heads. / Seeing the two exceedingly skilled in singing, people were astonished; / they were skilled in the distinctions of notes: ṣaḍja, madhyama, and gāndhāra.
Beholding them so capable, through the yoga of knowledge of the future / I had them sing the auspicious, captivating Rāmāyaṇa that I had composed.
Skilled in the mṛdaṅga, paṇava, and other instruments, as well as the vīṇā, / singing in forest after forest, they enchanted the beasts and birds.
To hear the wondrous sweetness of the singing of your two boys, O Rāma, / Varuṇa brought those two children at night.
Charming in age and form, having crossed the ocean of the art of song, / the two boys sang sweetly there at the command of the lord of the realm.
Your supreme, sweet, lovely, and holy story / Varuṇa heard, together with his household and the singers.
Listening together with Mitra, Varuṇa was not at all sated; / for sweeter even than nectar is your story, O son of Raghu.
His breath and bodily functions stolen away by intense greed for the bliss of their singing, / he did not at all command the two boys of yours to return.
Though enticed by delightful, great luxuries, the two boys / did not waver, due to their remembrance of their guru’s and their mother’s lotus feet.
And I, too, went afterward to Varuṇa’s supreme abode; / with love, Varuṇa offered me worship, O lord.
Though he is all-knowing, he questioned me regarding the two boys' birth, deeds, and the like; / and I told Varuṇa everything: their birth, their acquisition of learning, and so on.
Hearing that they were Sītā’s sons, the god honored them with garments and ornaments; / out of respect for my words, [he said,] ‘Given by a god, this is to be accepted.’

What was given by Varuṇa, pleased with the qualities of their instrumental playing, singing, learning, and youth, / was taken by the two princes. / Then the accomplished Varuṇa spoke to me regarding Sītā:
‘Sītā is the foremost of devoted wives, endowed with beauty, virtue, and youth, / the mother of heroic sons, most blessed; she does not deserve abandonment under any circumstances.
Indeed, great loss comes from abandoning her, O son of Raghu; / for she is your supreme accomplishment among accomplishments, truly unfailing.
If her greatness is not acknowledged by vulgar people who are corrupt, / what loss is there in that, O Rāma, whose listening and praising brings merit?
Her holy conduct is ever witnessed by us; / those who contemplate Sītā’s feet attain success at once.
By her mere intention, the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and other functions / of the worlds, which belong to the Supreme Lord, take place eternally.
Sītā is death, and she is nectar; she burns, and she rains; / heaven, liberation, asceticism, yoga, and generosity—Jānakī is all these to you.
Brahmā, Śiva, and the other world guardians, along with pride and so on— / she creates them, she alone creates them; no other is your beloved Sītā.
You are the father of all the worlds, and Sītā is the mother; therefore, / a wicked view here is by no means suitable for your well-being at any time.
You yourself, the all-knowing Bhagavat, know Sītā to be ever pure; / even you [regard] the daughter of the earth as dearer than life itself.
Therefore, Jānakī, being pure, should be honored by you as your beloved; / and there is no defeat through a curse upon Sītā or upon you, O all-pervading lord.
These words of mine must be spoken by you directly to Rāma, / the master of the worlds, O Vālmīki, best of sages!’
'Thus was I addressed by Varuṇa, for the purpose of taking Sītā back; / and in the very same way by all the world-protectors as well, O lord.'
the singing of the Rāmāyaṇa by your two sons was heard by gods, asuras, / and all gandharvas, their minds seized with wonder.
Delighted, all of them praised your two sons; / the three worlds were captivated by the two of them through their virtues of form, song, and age.
Whatever was given by the world guardians was indeed accepted by your two sons; / from the ṛṣis came boons to them both, and from the others fame alone.
Formerly, the whole world was seen by the sage as having only one Rāma; / now, through your two sons, it has become three Rāmas in the sight of all.
Formerly in the world, an ultimate form of one Kāma was seen; / but today, through the four desires, this [world] appears in every way.
Everywhere else, O king of kings, the two sons of Rāma, Kuśa and Lava, / are praised in song; why is restraint shown here toward you, who are wise?
In all your deeds great praise is heard, / except for the abandonment of Sītā, O crest-jewel of those of virtuous renown!
By you, the master of the three worlds who are imitating the householder’s life, / the two sons endowed with learning, virtue, and good qualities must be acknowledged, O Rāma.
Abandoning their mother, the two would not stay near your presence; / therefore, the two sons should be summoned by you together with their mother.
Now, by reviving the army, you have once again given / conviction to all the worlds—a conviction that purifies even those who are fallen.
Neither our name nor the gods' was unknown to him, O giver of honor; / in her purity, however, what was lost to the worlds is now certainly restored here.”
Śeṣa said: / Thus addressed by Vālmīki, Rāma, though omniscient, having praised / and bowed to Vālmīki, replied to Lakṣmaṇa:
“Go now, dear brother, to bring Sītā who practices dharma, / along with our sons, mounting a chariot together with Sumantra, O friend.
Having recited these words of mine and of the sage, / and having consoled her, bring that Sītā back swiftly to this city.”
Lakṣmaṇa said: / “I will go at your command, O lord, sovereign over all of us; / if the queen comes, O lord, then my journey will be fruitful.
May that virtuous lady not harbor resentment toward me because of my past fault! / But if she does not come, forgive my coming back [empty-handed].”
Having spoken thus to Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa stood on his chariot by the king's command / and, accompanied by Sumitra and the sage's disciples, went to the hermitage of the earth-born [Sītā].
[He thought,] “How can the revered lady Sītā be propitiated by me, / knowing the past fault of me, who am always dependent upon Rāma?”
Reflecting thus within himself, caught between joy and hesitation, / Lakṣmaṇa reached Sītā’s hermitage, which dispels all weariness.
Descending from the chariot near her, his eyes blocked with tears, / crying repeatedly, “O noble lady, O venerable one, O revered one, O auspicious one!”,
he fell at her feet, his entire body trembling; / and he was raised up by that queen, overwhelmed with affection.
“For what purpose have you come, gentle one, to the forest dear to sages? / Is the lord well, that pearl from the oyster-shell of Kausalyā?
Is there any anger in him toward me? Does he respect only his fame? / And is he praised by all the worlds as an ocean of auspicious qualities?
Fearing infamy, he appointed you to abandon me; / has his fame in the worlds become spotless as a result?
Even if I die, having secured my husband’s good renown firmly, / may closeness to my husband be mine swiftly, O brother-in-law!
Even though abandoned by him, he was not abandoned by me in the slightest; / for the fruit depends on the means, but the cause does not depend on the fruit.
Is Kausalyā, free from grief, ever full of compassion toward me, / doing well—she whose son is the protector of the three worlds?
Are all my kinsmen, Bharata and the others, well, / and the noble Sumitrā, to whom I am dearer than life?
Were you too, like me, abandoned for the sake of fame in all the worlds? / What is hard to abandon for that king to whom even his own self is not dear?”
Thus questioned in many ways by her, Rāma's younger brother, [honoured by] the virtuous, / said: 'The lord is well, and he inquires after your well-being.'
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and the other royal ladies / have asked after your welfare with affection, O queen, along with blessings.
Preceded by inquiries after your welfare, I report to you / the salutation to your feet made by Śatrughna and Bharata, O auspicious lady.
By the elders and by all the wives of the elders, O auspicious Jānakī, / blessings have been given, and inquiries after your welfare have been made.
The self-controlled lord calls you sincerely; / delight elsewhere cannot be attained by him apart from you, O passionate lady!”

‘Seeing all directions empty without you, O daughter of Janaka,
our lord weeps, making others weep as well.

Wherever you dwell, O queen, Rāghava always remembers you;
he regards that place alone as not empty, O daughter of Videha.

“Blessed is this hermitage of Vālmīki where Jānakī
spends her time talking of news of me!”—so he says.

Hear what our lord, while weeping, said concerning you;
for that which is in the speaker's heart undoubtedly becomes manifest:

“People call me alone the lord of all lords;
but I declare their own unseen destiny to be the independent cause.

Even the lord of all merely follows destiny in deeds;
why should those who are ruled not follow it in joy and sorrow?

In the breaking of the bow, in Kaikeyī's loss of sense, in my father's death,
in going to the forest, there in your abduction, in crossing the ocean,

in the slaying of the lord of the rākṣasas in battle after battle,
in the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas becoming my allies,

in the recovery of you, O jewel of faithful wives, in keeping my vow true,
in reuniting with my kinsmen, and in regaining the kingdom, O lady,

and again in separation from my beloved—that which was the irresistible cause
has now become gracious today towards our reunion once again.

He by whom the Veda was otherwise arranged, from whom are the creation and dissolution of the world—
because I follow the worlds, therefore am I the first cause.

The worlds follow destiny, which brings realization;
destiny is exhausted through experience, and that has been experienced by you in the forest.

My uncaused love for you, O Sītā, which ever increases,
has respectfully summoned you, setting aside the destiny of the world.

An immersion in the purity of love occurs
even through a suspected fault; thus is it truly pure, ever to be savored by the wise.

This purification of love, O auspicious one, was done by me in your regard, not otherwise;
moreover, this world had to be protected by one who follows the conduct of the virtuous.

It was for purification in all conditions through censure of us two, O queen;
for this world, confounded, would perish through the conduct of the great.

Splendid is our fame, splendid is our love,
splendid are our two lineages, and splendid are our deeds.

May the singers of our fame be radiant upon earth;
those who have devotion toward us two cross over the ocean of worldly existence in the end.”
'You have been spoken of thus by him, who is pleased with your virtues: / let her turn her compassionate mind toward seeing her husband's lotus feet.'

Delightful garments, magnificent ornaments,
body ointment, and charming perfumes have been provided for you.

A chariot and maidservants have been sent by Rāma for your festive journey,
as well as an umbrella, two bright fly-whisks, elephants, and horses, O radiant lady.

Praised by the foremost twice-born, by heralds, bards, and panegyrists,
saluted by the women of the city, and attended by warriors,

showered with flowers, O queen, by celestial nymphs and others,
giving wealth as desired to the twice-born,

placing both young princes mounted on an elephant in front, O ruler of the people,
and followed by me, go to your own city, Ayodhyā.

When you have gone there and are united with your beloved,
among all the royal women who have assembled from everywhere,

and all the wives of the sages, and the people of Kosala as well,
let there be a great festival today with auspicious musical instruments, songs, and the like.’

Śeṣa said:
Having heard this petition, Queen Sītā said to him:
‘I do not bring fame to the king; indeed, I myself am his ill fame.

What could be accomplished by him through me, who am devoid of dharma, desire, and wealth?
Such being the case, what trust can there be in your king, who is unrestrained?

Direct or indirect, the faults of a husband present in the mind
must never be spoken by one like me, born of an auspicious lineage.

That form which resided in my heart at the time of the wedding
never departs from this heart.

O Lakṣmaṇa, these two princes of mine, born of his radiant portion,
the shoots of his lineage, are great heroes, skilled in the science of archery.

Having brought them to their father, they should be carefully cherished;
remaining here, I shall willingly worship Rāma through ascetic penance.

O fortunate one, salutation to his venerable feet
and well-being to all must be spoken by you having gone from here on my behalf.’
Sītā instructed her two sons: 'Go into your father's presence; / he who grants his own realm must indeed be served by you both.'

Though commanded, those two young princes, Kuśa and Lava, were unwilling;
yet by the word of Vālmīki they went there along with Lakṣmaṇa.

The two sons went to the lotus feet of Vālmīki;
Lakṣmaṇa also, having gone along with the boys, saluted him.

Vālmīki, Lakṣmaṇa, and the two princes, having met together,
went eagerly, knowing that Rāma was sitting in the royal assembly.

Then the wise Lakṣmaṇa, having bowed down,
told everything to Rāma, beginning with Sītā’s words, filled with joy and sorrow.

From the words of Sītā’s message, Rāma fell into a faint;
and having regained consciousness, he said to Lakṣmaṇa, who was skilled in prudent conduct:

‘Go again there, O friend, with great effort,
and quickly bring her back, communicating my words, may good fortune be yours:

“In the forest, performing asceticism, has some other recourse been contemplated,
heard of, or seen by you other than me, that you do not come, O Jānakī?

By your own desire alone you went from here to the forest dear to sages;
those wives of the sages were honored, and the hosts of sages were seen by you.

Your wish has been fulfilled today; why do you not come, O lady?
You should see no fault in me, looking at your own desire.

Having gone and gone, or rather, O woman of fair thighs, the husband alone is the refuge of a woman;
even if devoid of qualities, he is an ocean of virtues—how much more one desired by her heart?

Whatever rite is performed by women of noble family, all that is for the satisfaction of the husband;
I was already satisfied before, and now am exceedingly so with you.

Sacrifice, muttering of mantras, asceticism, charity, vows, sacred pilgrimage sites, compassion, and the like—
and the gods—are satisfied without a doubt when I am satisfied.”’

Śeṣa said:
Taking this message from the lord of the universe for Sītā,
Lakṣmaṇa said to his lord, bowing out of affection for Hari:

‘Concerning the bringing of Sītā, that which you, being gracious, have spoken,
that word I shall convey, endowed with humility.’
Having said this and bowed at the feet of Raghunātha, Lakṣmaṇa / departed swiftly to Sītā, standing in his chariot of great speed.

Seeing the two sons of Rāma possessed of splendour and great vigour,
Vālmīki, assuming a smile and making a delightful countenance, said:

‘Sing, O my two sons, the wonderful life of Rāma,
playing the vīṇā, adorned with melodious singing!’
Having been instructed thus, the two illustrious sons / sang the deeds of Rāma, which bestow great merit, adorned with excellent words and phrases.

in which the rule of dharma is visibly present and wifely fidelity abides,
where there is great brotherly love, and likewise devotion to the preceptor,

where proper conduct between master and servant is indeed personified,
where punishment is dealt to evildoers directly by the foremost of the Raghus.

The world was pervaded by that singing; even the gods in heaven stood [spellbound];
even the kinnaras, having heard that song, instantly went into a trance.

Hearing the sound of the vīṇā, adorned with meter and rhythm,
the entire assembly there became motionless like carved statues.
Shedding tears of joy, Rāma and the other kings / were captivated by the song in the pañcama melody, like figures in a painting.
Seeing his two sons there, charming everyone with their great singing, / Rāma gave each of them separately a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Seeing Vālmīki, the best of sages, intent on taking it, / the two smiling boys spoke to him then, their eyebrows slightly arched:
"O sage, a great injustice is indeed committed by this king, / since he wishes to give gold to the two of us, enticing us with greed!
Acceptance of gifts is praised for Brahmins, not for others; / a king devoted to receiving gifts is fit only for hell.
The ruler of the earth enjoys his kingdom abandoned through our kindness; / why does he wish to give gold, heaped up with auspicious merits?"
Seeing them having spoken thus, Vālmīki, filled with compassion, / praised them: 'You two, who are foremost in knowing statecraft, should know [him as] your father.'
Hearing the sage's words, the two boys, filled with humility / and exceedingly pure through devotion to their mother, clung to the king's feet.
Rāma, filled with joy, embraced both boys firmly against his body, / and considered that the two dharmas of his wife had appeared before him in bodily form.
Even the assembly, beholding the charming faces of Rāma's two sons, / considered her devotion to the lord of Jānakī to be true, O best of sages.
Hearing this uttered from the mouth of Śeṣa, Vātsyāyana, / wishing to hear the Rāmāyaṇa endowed with all virtues, said:
Vātsyāyana said: / "At what time, O master, was this great Rāmāyaṇa composed? / For what reason did he compose it, and what is described therein? Tell me that!"
Śeṣa said: / Once the Brahmin Vālmīki went to a great forest / where there were palm trees, tamāla trees, and blossoming kiṃśuka trees;
where the ketakī with its pollen made the forest fragrant, / and appeared great like moonlight, bearing white spikes, / and where there were campaka, bakula, kovidāra, and kuraṇṭaka trees;
where many trees were in bloom in that beautiful forest, / resounding all around with the cries of cuckoos / and the humming of bees,
delightful, filled with charming youthfulness. / There a lovely pair of krauñca birds, afflicted by the arrow of desire,
delighting in each other, sported, joined in affection. / Then a hunter arrived and, craving a taste of meat,
a pitiless man killed one of the two, the charming [male]. / Then the female krauñca bird, seeing her mate killed by the hunter, afflicted with sorrow,
lamented bitterly out of grief, crying aloud. / Then the sage, enraged, touched the pure, auspicious water of the river
and cursed the Niṣāda, the killer of the krauñca bird: / "May you not attain a resting place for eternal years, O Niṣāda,
since you have killed one of the krauñca birds infatuated with desire!" / Then, realizing that a metrical verse composition had been produced, the Brahmins
delightedly spoke to the sage, praising him, "Well done! Well done! / O master, when you uttered the curse in words, the goddess of speech unfolded a verse!
This verse is exceedingly enchanting, O best of sages!" / Then the sage's heart was filled with joy, O bull among Brahmins. / At that time, Brahmā arrived accompanied by his sons,
and spoke these words to Vālmīki: "Fortunate are you, O best of sages! / The goddess of speech, dwelling in your mouth, has attained the state of verse.
Therefore, compose the delightful Rāmāyaṇa in sweet syllables, / through which your spotless fame will endure until the end of the cosmic age.
Blessed indeed is that speech on the tongue which is united with Rāma's name; / any other tale of passion only generates sin for men.
Therefore compose the deeds of Rāma, renowned throughout the world, / by which the destruction of sinners' sins will occur at every step."
Having spoken thus, the Creator, accompanied by all the gods, vanished; / then he pondered, 'How could the Rāmāyaṇa come to be?'
Then, intent on meditation on the lovely bank of the river, / the enchanting Rāma appeared in his mind.
Beholding Rāma, dark as a blue lotus petal, lotus-eyed, / and seeing his past, future, and present deeds,
he attained exceeding joy, and then composed the Rāmāyaṇa, / endowed with charming words and manifold meters.
In that Rāmāyaṇa there are six highly delightful books, O sinless one: / the Bāla, the Āraṇyaka, and the other, the Kiṣkindhā, as well as the Sundara,
the Yuddha, and the other, the Uttara; these six, O man of great wisdom. / Whichever man hears them out of merit is freed from all sins.
There, in the Bāla[kāṇḍa], Paṅktiratha, pleased through the sacrifice for sons, / obtained four sons, the eternal Brahman, Hari in person.
Going to Kauśika's sacrifice, marrying Sītā, [meeting] the descendant of Bhṛgu, / returning to the city, the excellent one's appointment as crown prince,
going to the forest on his mother's word, crossing the Gaṅgā, to Mount / Citrakūṭa together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa—
prudent Bharata, hearing of his brother in the forest, went there; / failing to obtain him, he himself took up residence in Nandigrāma.
Hear this Bāla[kāṇḍa]; hear another arising from the forest: / residence in the hermitage of sages and descriptions there in various places;
the cutting off of Śūrpaṇakhā's nose, the destruction of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, / the slaying of the illusory Mārīca, the abduction of the woman by the demon;
his wandering in the forest as an abandoned lover, carrying out human conduct; / the beholding of Kabandha there, and likewise going to Pampā;
the union with Hanūmat: this is designated the Forest [Book]. / Listen also to the other, O sage; I shall recount it in brief:
the piercing of the seven palm trees, and the wondrous slaying of Vālin, / the bestowal of kingship upon Sugrīva, and the description of the mountain;
the message concerning the task from Lakṣmaṇa, the dispatching of Sugrīva, / likewise the summoning of the army, and also the search for Sītā;
the beholding of Sampāti there, and likewise the leaping across the ocean, / the monkey's arrival on the other shore: that is the wondrous Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa.
Hear of the Sundarakāṇḍa, where the wondrous story of Rāma is: / the monkey's wanderings into house after house, the sight of wonders;
the sight of Sītā there, and conversation with Jānakī; / the destruction of the grove, and the binding of the monkey by the enraged [demons];
then the setting of Laṅkā on fire, then the reunion with the monkeys, / the presentation of Rāma's token of recognition, and the departure of the army;
the building of the bridge on the ocean, the encounter with Śuka and Sāraṇa; / thus the Sundara is recounted; in the Yuddha, the reunion with Sītā;
in the Uttara, the conversation of the ṛṣis, and the beginning of the sacrifice; / therein are many stories of Rāma that destroy the sins of those who hear them.
Thus the six books that dispel the guilt of killing a brāhmaṇa have been related; / in brief have they been told by me to you, exceedingly charming.
Consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, marked by six books: / that indeed is declared the Rāmāyaṇa, destroying the greatest sins.
Having heard that, Rāghava, delighted, placed his two sons on a seat; / embracing the two firmly, he then remembered his beloved Sītā.

5.67.m: Śeṣa said: / Then Saumitri, having arrived, bowed down repeatedly to Jānakī, / declaring with a voice choked with love the word inspired by Rāma.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa arrived and endowed with humility, / and hearing Rāma's message from his mouth, Sītā, feeling bashful, said:
“O Saumitri, how could I come, abandoned by Rāma in the great forest? / I remain here in Vālmīki's hermitage, remembering Rāma.”
Hearing the words spoken from her mouth, Saumitri said: / “O mother, devoted wife, Rāma summons you repeatedly.
A devoted wife does not hold in her heart a fault committed by her husband. / Therefore, do come with me, mounting this excellent chariot.”
Hearing these and other words, Jānakī, who held her husband as her deity, / cast aside the anger in her mind and stood on the chariot with the son of Sumitrā.
Bowing to all the ascetic women and the sages resplendent with the Vedas, / remembering Rāma in her mind, she stood in the chariot and departed for the city.
In due course she reached the city, adorned with priceless ornaments, / and arrived at the river Sarayū where Rāma himself was staying.
Alighting from the chariot along with Lakṣmaṇa, the graceful [Sītā], / entirely devoted to her husband, grasped Rāma's feet.
Rāma, seeing Jānakī arrived, overwhelmed with love, [said:] / “O virtuous woman, with you now I shall complete the sacrifice.”
Having bowed to Vālmīki and likewise to the other best of Brahmins, / she went, eager to pay homage at the feet of the mothers.
Then Kauśalyā, seeing dear Jānakī approaching, the mother of heroic sons, / showered her with blessings and experienced manifold joy.
Kaikeyī, seeing the daughter of the king of Videha bowing at her feet, / bestowed a blessing: “May you live long with your husband and with your sons!”
Sumitrā, seeing the daughter of the king of Videha bowing at her feet, / bestowed upon her a blessing granting sons and grandsons.
Having bowed to all of them, Sītā, the chaste and beloved wife of Rāmacandra, / was filled with supreme joy, indeed, O Brahmin.
Seeing Rāmacandra's wife arrived, the jar-born [Agastya] / set aside the golden effigy of his wife and placed her, the practitioner of dharma, [beside him].
Then Rāma shone in the midst of the sacrifice together with Sītā, / like the moon accompanied by a star, radiant in autumn.
When the delightful time arrived, he performed the ritual procedure there / with the daughter of the king of Videha, the practitioner of dharma, which removes all sins.
Seeing Rāma engaged in the sacrificial rite together with Sītā, / [the people] there rejoiced, filled with curiosity.
Rāma said to wise Vasiṣṭha at that excellent sacrifice: / “O master, what must be done by me that is of the utmost necessity?”
Hearing Rāma's words, the highly intelligent guru said: / “A worship that brings satisfaction should be performed for the Brahmins.
Formerly, a sacrifice was instituted by Marutta, furnished with provisions; / the Brahmins were satisfied there at that time with wealth and other gifts.
The Brahmins were not able to carry away the immense burden of wealth; / the twice-born, unable to endure the load of wealth, cast it down in the Himavat region.
Therefore you too, foremost of kings, wealthy and best of monarchs, / give gifts and the like to the Brahmins so that highest satisfaction may arise.”
Hearing this, that foremost of kings, regarding the jar-born [Agastya] as worthy of honor, / first honored the son of Brahmā, rich in asceticism,
with heaps of manifold gems, with many loads of gold, / and with lands populated with people, which bestowed supreme pleasure.
He honored the charming Agastya along with his wife / likewise with jewels, gold, and also various territories.
He similarly honored Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī; / he honored Cyavana together with his wife with fine gems.
He also honored all the other sages, the officiating priests, treasures of asceticism, / with multitudes of jewels and manifold loads of gold.
Then at the sacrifice Rāma gave abundant sacrificial fees to the Brahmins: / a hundred thousand pieces of gold to each twice-born.
And to the poor, the blind, and the destitute he gave gifts in manifold ways, / with delightful wealth and gems offered to their satisfaction.
Various garments and soft foods / he bestowed there according to the scriptures, bringing pleasure to all.
Crowded with joyful and well-fed people, filled with all living beings, / the city, filled with men and women, became exceedingly glad.
Seeing him giving gifts to all, the sage born from a jar, / the twice-born, experienced supreme delight at that excellent sacrifice.
Then, to fetch water like nectar for the consecrated bath, / he summoned sixty-four kings accompanied by their wives.
Rāma, along with Sītā, went to fetch the water / with a golden-colored jar, resplendent with every ornament.
Saumitri also went with Urmilā; King Bharata with Māṇḍavī; / Śatrughna with Śrutakīrti; and Puṣkala with Kāntimatī;
Subāhu with Satyavatī; Satyavat with Vīrabhūṣā; / Sumada with Satkīrti; and King Vimala with his queen;
King Vīramaṇi with charming Śrutavatī; / Lakṣmīnidhi with Komalā; Riputāpa with Aṅgasenā;
Vibhīṣaṇa with Mahāmūrti; Pratāpāgrya with Pratītā; / Ugrāśva with Kāmagamā; Nīlaratnoddhi with Ramyā;
Suratha with Sumanohārī; and likewise the monkey [Sugrīva] with Mohanā; / these and other kings the Brahmin sage Vasiṣṭha dispatched.
Going to the Sarayū, overflowing with auspicious and sacred waters, / Vasiṣṭha, knower of mantras, consecrated the water with Vedic mantras:
“O water, purify this steed with water that captivates the mind, / for the sacrifice of Rāmacandra, the sole protector of all the worlds.”
All the kings, Rāma and the others, brought that water touched by the sage / into the sacrificial hall, which was being praised by the best of Brahmins.
Bathing the horse, white as milk, with the pure waters, / the jar-born [Agastya] consecrated it with a mantra through Rāma's hand:
“Purify me, O great steed, in this [sacrifice] crowded with Brahmins; / through your sacrificial offering, may all the gods be gratified and pleased.”
Having spoken thus, King Rāma touched [the sacrificial materials] together with Sītā; / then all the twice-born regarded it as a wonder out of curiosity.
They said to one another: “By remembering whose name men / are liberated from great sin, what is that Rāma saying? Ah!”
When King Rāma had spoken thus, the jar-born sage / consecrated a sword with mantras and placed it in Rāma's hand.
When the sword was held and touched by Rāma at the sacrifice, / that horse swiftly abandoned its animal state and assumed a celestial form.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, surrounded on all sides by apsarases, / fanned with chowries, and adorned with a garland of victory,
then all the people at the sacrifice, seeing him having shed the state of a horse / and bearing a splendid celestial form, were filled with astonishment.
Then Rāma, knowing [the truth] himself but wishing to reveal it to all people, / the supremely righteous one questioned that deity of celestial form:
“Who are you that have attained a celestial body? Why had you fallen into the state of a horse? / How is it that you are accompanied by celestial women? What do you wish to do? Tell me that.”
Hearing Rāma's words, the deity replied to the protector of the earth, / smiling, speaking charming words with a voice like the rumble of a cloud:
“Nothing is unknown to you, who move within and without everything. / Nevertheless, since you ask, I shall tell you as it truly is.”
In a former birth, O Rāma, I was a twice-born man of supreme righteousness; / yet I acted contrary to the Veda, O scorcher of foes.
Once of old, I went to the bank of the Dhūtapāpā river, / which was delightful with many trees and pleasing everywhere to the mind.
Having bathed there, satisfied the ancestors, and given gifts according to the ritual rules, / I performed meditation upon you, O mighty-armed one, conforming to the Vedas.
Then many people arrived there, O king; / for the purpose of deceiving them, I practiced this hypocrisy.
A splendid courtyard filled with materials for many sacrifices, / covered with garments, charming, and furnished with sacrificial rings and the like, a great sight—
the smoke rising from the Agnihotra on all sides / made the courtyard of the sky incomparably lovely, assuming a wondrous form.
With limbs adorned by the splendor of many tilakas, performing great austerities, / graced with darbha grass, with fuel sticks in hand, I seemed to be hypocrisy incarnate.
Wandering the surface of the earth at his own will, / the greatly radiant Durvāsas arrived there on the bank of the Dhūtapāpā river.
He saw me performing hypocrisy, maintaining silence before him, / not offering him respectful water, acting insolent, and uttering no words of welcome.
Seeing this, that wise sage was overcome with intense anger, like the ocean on the full moon, / and he severely cursed me, the hypocrite:
‘Since you practice hypocrisy on the bank of the river, O very wicked-minded one, / therefore obtain the unspeakable state of a beast, O vile ascetic!’
Hearing the curse that was pronounced, I then became sorrowful; / I indeed grasped the feet of that sage Durvāsas.
Then, O Rāma, the twice-born sage granted me an excellent favor: / ‘Attain the state of a horse at the sacrifice of the king of kings, O ascetic;
thereafter, by the touch of his hand, go to that supreme abode, / having assumed a divine, heart-captivating form devoid of hypocrisy.’
Because of that, even the curse that was pronounced has become a blessing to me, / in that I obtained the delightful touch of your hand.
That very touch of your fingers, which is difficult to attain by gods and others through many births, / I have attained here, difficult though it is to obtain.
Grant permission, O great king; by your grace / I go to that great eternal abode of yours, free from sorrow and the like,
where there is no grief, no old age, no death, no delusion of time; / to that abode I go, O lord of men, by your grace.’
Having spoken thus and circumambulated him, he mounted an excellent celestial vehicle, / encrusted with many jewels and praised by all the gods.
He went to the eternal abode by the grace of Rāma’s feet, / a place without return, free from sorrow and delusion.
Having heard what was told by him and recognizing Rāma, the other people / were all struck with wonder, beside themselves with joy toward one another.
Listen, O twice-born one of great intellect: even when remembered through hypocrisy, Hari / grants liberation completely—how much more so when free from hypocrisy!
Somehow or other, the supreme remembrance of Rāma must be made, / by which one attains the supreme abode, difficult even for gods and others to attain.
Beholding that marvel, the sages considered themselves to have achieved their purpose, / having been purified by the sight of Rāma’s feet and the touch of his hand.
When that god, who had formerly assumed the form of a horse, had gone to heaven, / Rāma spoke to the treasuries of austerities, the best knowers of the Veda:
‘What should be done by me, O brāhmaṇa? The horse has disappeared, gone comfortably; / how shall the oblation take place before us, satisfying all the deities?
Let the sages act in such a way that the gods are completely satisfied, / so that my sacrifice is supreme, and my ritual conforms to what is prescribed in scripture.’
Hearing these words, the best of sages, / Vasiṣṭha, who was skilled in discerning the minds of all the gods, spoke:
‘Bring camphor quickly, by which the gods themselves, / having received the oblation of old, will now accept it, urged on by my word.’
Hearing these words, Rāma quickly offered / much camphor, exceedingly beautiful, for the pleasure of the gods.
Then the sage, delighted in spirit, invoked the wondrous gods; / they all arrived at that very moment, accompanied by their entourages.

5.68.m: Śeṣa said: / Indra there, relishing the sweet oblation beheld by Rāmacandra / at the sacrifice, did not attain satiety together with the gods.
Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, the four-faced Brahmā there, / Varuṇa, Kubera, and likewise the other guardians of the worlds,
having tasted the smooth oblation prepared by Vasiṣṭha there, / indeed [stood] there again, O best of twice-borns, like hungry men from a feast.
Having satisfied all the gods with the oblation, the treasury of compassion, / urged on by Vasiṣṭha, performed all that was to be done.
The brāhmaṇas were satisfied with gifts, the best gods were pleased with the oblation; / all of them, being gratified, took their share and went to their own abode.
To the sages and the foremost hotṛ priests he gave the kingdom in the four quarters; / satisfied, those twice-born ones gave blessings of good fortune to Rāma.
Then, having performed the final oblation, Vasiṣṭha said to the noble women: / ‘Congratulate the lord of the earth, the supreme completer of the sacrifice.’
Hearing his speech, those women joyfully scattered parched grain over him / who surpassed the god of love in beauty, adorned with great jewels.
Then he directed the king for the final purificatory bath; / Rāma went together with his own people to the excellent bank of the Sarayū.
Surrounded by many millions of kings traveling on foot, / he went to that best of rivers, crowded with flocks of birds.
Just as the lord of the stars, possessed of radiance, shines surrounded by his own wives, / so did Rāma shine resplendent, surrounded by the hosts of kings.
Learning of that festival, people went in haste, / their eyes transfixed upon beholding the face of Sītā’s husband.
Beholding the lord of kings going toward the river together with Sītā, / the people, longing for a long time for the sight, were delighted.
Many actors and Gandharvas, singing radiant fame, / followed the lord of the earth, who is saluted by all the worlds.
Dancing girls dancing there, agitating the mind of the master, / and sprinkling with water syringes, went to attend upon glorious Rāma.
Anointing the great king with turmeric, saffron, and other unguents, / and smearing one another, they attained very great joy.
splendid with pearl necklaces placed upon their pairs of breasts, / distinguished by golden earrings that brushed against their pairs of ears;
Proceeding along the road crowded with many men and women, / he duly reached the river overflowing with auspicious, holy water.
Having gone there, the lotus-eyed Rāma with Vaidehī, / accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and others, entered the holy water.
All the kings and the multitudes of people entered after him / into the water purified by the dust of his feet, worshiped by all the worlds.
Sprinkling one another with delightful water syringes, / all of them with very red eyes experienced supreme joy in their minds.
Having sported for a long time amid the waves of the river in the flood of holy water / together with Sītā, Rāma came out, endowed with righteousness.

Clad in silk garments, with crown and earrings, endowed with beautiful armlets and excellent bracelets,
bearing the splendor of ten million gods of love, the king shone forth, praised by the foremost of kings.

Having erected a sacrificial post adorned with finest colors on the best riverbank, that noble-minded king
attained by his own arms the wondrous splendor of the three worlds, hard to be attained by others.

Performing thus three horse sacrifices together with the daughter of Janaka,
he attained matchless renown throughout the three worlds, very difficult even for gods to attain.

Thus, dear one, has been described to you the noble tale of Rāma about which I was asked.
The sacrifice has been told in detail; what else do you ask, O twice-born one?

Whoever listens with devotion to Hari to the excellent sacrifice of Rāmacandra,
having instantly crossed over the [sin of] killing a brahmin, will attain the eternal Brahman.

One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one bound is freed from bondage.

Since by hearing this tale even a wicked outcaste attains the highest station,
how much more so the foremost of brahmins who is devoted to the worship of Rāma?

By remembering the fortunate Rāma, even sinners can attain the highest station,
the supreme heaven, difficult to attain even for Śakra and the other gods.

Blessed are those mortals in the world who remember the best of the Raghus;
they, crossing over worldly existence in an instant, go to imperishable bliss.

Each single syllable is a forest fire to the bamboo grove of [the sin of] killing a brahmin.
The wise man should worship that teacher who recites it [to him].
Having heard the story, one should give a pair of cows to the narrator / and his wife, having worshipped [them] with clothes, ornaments, and food.

Two splendid, excellent golden images of Rāma and Sītā,
shining with earrings and adorned with signet-rings,

having been made, are indeed to be given to the reciter, O best of the twice-born;
then his gods and his ancestors would reach Vaikuṇṭha.

The tale of Rāma that was asked by you was told to you by me formerly.
What else, O wise brahmin, should be told before you?

Those who listen to this tale that destroys the multitude of sins of killing a brahmin
go to the highest abode, which is very hard to attain even for the gods.

Even a cow-killer, a son-killer, a liquor-drinker, or a violator of the guru's bed
becomes instantly purified indeed; here there is no room for doubt.

5.69.m:
The sages said:
Fully has Rāma's horse sacrifice been heard from you, O fortunate one!
Now tell the glorification of the great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Sūta said:
Let the tiger-like sages hear the nectar-like deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
which Śivā asked of the Lord of beings, and which I shall proclaim to you.

Once the goddess Pārvatī, her mind full of affection for Śiva,
having bowed down with love, spoke this word:

Pārvatī said:
Of the infinite millions of universes, and of what stands outside and within them,
the highest abode of Viṣṇu is chief, supreme, and best among them.

Beyond which there is no beloved, delightful abode of Kṛṣṇa—
all that I wish to hear; tell it to me, O great Lord!

The Lord said:
More secret than the secret, secret, producing supreme bliss,
a most wondrous, hidden abode, bliss supreme of the supreme,

and the most difficult to attain among those hard to attain, supreme enchanter,
full of all potencies, O goddess, concealed in all places,

the uppermost abode of the Sātvatas, exceedingly hard to reach even for Viṣṇu,
eternal, named Vṛndāvana, situated above the universe.

It has the complete bliss and sovereignty of Brahman, eternal, imperishable bliss;
Vaikuṇṭha and the like are fractions of its parts, while Vṛndāvana itself is on earth.

Whatever sovereignty of Goloka there is, that is established in Gokula;
whatever majesty of Vaikuṇṭha there is, that is established in Dvārikā;

that supreme majesty of Brahman, however, eternally resorts to Vṛndāvana;
the supreme realm of Kṛṣṇa is especially in the midst of the forest among them.

Therefore, the earth is renowned as blessed in the midst of the three worlds,
because that named after Mathurā is exclusively dear to Viṣṇu.
Its own region is the superior entity named the circle of Mathurā, / a secret and diverse abode situated within the city.
The circle of Mathurā has the shape of a thousand-petalled lotus, / a marvelous Vaiṣṇava abode revolving around the discus of Viṣṇu.
Its pericarp and the spread of its petals are declared to be the secret tree. / Its glorification of the twelve chief forests is spoken of in order:
Bhadra, Śrī, Loha, Bhāṇḍīra, Mahātāla, and Khadīra; / Bakula, Kumuda, Kāmya, Madhu, and likewise Vṛndāvana.
Twelve is the count of these: seven to the west of the Yamunā, / and five forests are proclaimed to the east; in them lies the supreme mystery.
The great forest named Gokula, and likewise Madhu and Vṛndāvana; / other secondary groves are declared to be places for the aesthetic joy of Kṛṣṇa's play:
Kadambakhaṇḍana, Nandavana, and likewise Nandīśvara, / Nandanandanakhaṇḍa, and Palāśa, Aśoka, Ketakī,
Sugandha, Mānasa, Kaila, Amṛta, the dining place, / Sukhaprasādhana, Vatsaharaṇa, and Śeṣaśāyin,
Śyāmapūrva, Udadhi-village, and Cakrabhānupura, / Saṃketa, Dvipada, and Bālakrīḍanadhūsara,
Kāmadruma, Sulalita, and the grove Utsuka, / the site of various kinds of playful delights, the site of the aesthetic joy of multiple pastimes,
sustained by the expanse of the serpent [Śeṣa], declared to be the secret tree, / the great realm named Gokula, a thousand-petaled lotus.
The pericarp is that great abode, the supreme place of Govinda; / above there, on a golden throne, it is adorned with a jeweled pavilion.
On the pericarp, petals are declared in order in the cardinal and intermediate directions. / The petal that is proclaimed in the south is the supreme, highest of the high secret,
On that petal is the great seat, impassable to the Nigamas and Āgamas, / hard to attain even by masters of yoga; and Gokula, which is the soul of all.
The second petal is in the southeast, likewise that secret petal: / Saṃketa and Dvipada, and two huts situated on its bank.
The eastern petal is the third, the principal and supreme place, / considered a hundredfold superior by contact with all holy baths beginning with the Gaṅgā.
The fourth petal is in the northeast, that realm situated on the seat of perfection: / a new cowherd woman by her spiritual effort may obtain Kṛṣṇa as her husband there.
The stealing of the clothes and ornaments is recounted as being on that petal. / In the north, the fifth is proclaimed, the best petal of all petals.
The petal of the twelve Adityas is right here, equal to the pericarp. / In the northwest is the sixth petal; there the lake of Kāliya is remembered.
It is called the petal highest of the high, the primary place. / And the most supreme petal is commemorated as the seventh in the west,
which grants to the hosts of the wives of the sacrificers their desired boon; / here even a demon obtained final liberation, difficult even for the gods to attain.
Right here is the delusion of Brahmā, the petal that brings the lake of Brahmā. / In the southwest is proclaimed the eighth petal, where Vyoma was slain,
and there the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the site of the aesthetic joy of diverse sports. / The eight-petalled [lotus] situated within the forest of Vṛndā is proclaimed as heard.
Glorious Vṛndāvana is delightful, circumambulated by the Yamunā; / the basis of the liṅga of Śiva named Gopīśvara is seen there.
Outside that is a sixteen-petalled [lotus] full of splendor for that Lord, / proclaimed in all directions, in clockwise order:
The great realm, the great abode, named the personal dwelling place of Mādhava. / The first single petal is the highest, equal in glorification to the pericarp.
There on Mount Govardhana, delightful, the refuge of eternal aesthetic joy, / on the pericarp is the great divine play, in the deep recesses of the aesthetic joy of that play,
